The trouble is that the clash does not pull on him at all. He sees it, he names it, and nothing follows. No discomfort. No repair. No need to pick a side.

"The vegetables." Aristotle is not calling him stupid. He is saying there is nothing left to say to him. Argument runs on words holding still. If a word means one thing, it rules out the opposite. So anyone who says anything meaningful has already agreed to the rule. That is why Aristotle never tries to prove it: any proof would have to use it.

So he does something else. He asks the man for one small thing: say something that means something. The moment he speaks, he is beaten — not by an argument, but by the act of speaking. Which is why the man who stays silent escapes. Settle on nothing and there is nothing to refute. He has not lost the argument. He has stepped out of it.

Here the argument does less than it looks. Aristotle has shown the position cannot be defended. He has not shown that nobody can live inside it. He treats the two as the same because of something he assumes and never proves: that anyone who can speak will want to be defensible. Drop that, and the vegetable stops being a far edge of being human. It becomes a place a person can end up.

Twenty-three centuries later, Orwell named the place. Doublethink — holding two beliefs that clash, knowing they clash, and not minding — is usually read as the least believable part of Nineteen Eighty-Four. It is not. Ordinary inconsistency runs like this: you notice, you wince, you fix one. That sequence is reason working. Doublethink keeps the noticing and drops the rest.

So what is given up is not logic. It is a rule you hold over yourself: your beliefs must answer to each other. That is why facts cannot reach it. A wrong belief can be corrected. A dropped rule cannot. A correction only bites where contradicting yourself still costs you something.

No government has to do this to you. Think what a day of endless claims — clashing, always refreshed — asks of a person who still keeps the rule: weigh every source, face every clash, change your mind. The rule was built for a world with few enough claims to sort out. Under a flood it is a bill nobody can pay. So it goes unpaid. Not by decision, but by the plain arithmetic of attention. It does not feel like losing your reason. It feels like sensible triage — handling what matters and letting the rest go. Nobody wakes up and gives up consistency. They just stop having time for it, and the loss never announces itself.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: You catch two of your own beliefs that do not fit. The small wince, and the fixing that follows, are not a failure of thinking. That is thinking.
Watch for the shrug instead: you see the clash, you name it as a clash, and nothing in you moves.
When a correction lands on you as lightly as the false claim did, more facts will not help. What has gone missing is the demand that your beliefs answer to each other.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: What you believe changes all the time, and matters less than you think. Whether you still test what you believe is the part that is hardest to get back once you drop it.

recall.q: Aristotle's man is not confused — he sees the contradiction. So what has he given up, and why can't facts fix it?
recall.a: Not logic, but a rule he held over himself: his beliefs must answer to each other. A correction only bites where contradicting yourself still costs you something. Once that cost is gone, a fact lands as lightly as the claim it corrects.

cards.title: The fast mind and the slow mind may be one machine
cards.body: Psychology's most famous idea about thinking is that the mind runs on two systems — one fast and gut-level, one slow and careful. A new book says there is only one system, with many settings that move on their own. Get the machine right, the book bets, and a theory of belief becomes testable too. The reviewer agrees the two-system view is in trouble — and says the book still does not land the blow.

sections.text:
For decades the picture looked clean. Half the mind is fast, gut-level, automatic. The other half is slow, careful, under your control. Psychologists call these Type 1 and Type 2 thinking, and the split now turns up almost everywhere in psychology and brain science. Whatever the exact line between the halves, the claim "is supposed to cut cognition itself in two" — to split thinking down the middle.

The skeptic opens. Surely we just believe what our reasoning tells us. You think something through, the conclusion arrives, you hold it. What is left to study?

The skipped step is the machine. Before you can say how reasoning turns into belief, you have to know what does the reasoning. And the bold two-system answer has been failing for years. It said the traits travel in packs: fast with automatic with gut-level, slow with careful with controlled. Researchers looked, and found thinking that is fast but careful, and slow but gut-level. The packs came apart.

So defenders retreated. Keep the split, but hang it on one property: one kind of thinking uses working memory — the small mental desk where you hold something while you work on it — and the other does not. Nothing about speed. Nothing about effort. This version is hard to disprove because it barely predicts anything. Joshua Mugg's book, From Human Reasoning to Belief, says that is the problem: one such model is "explanatorily and predictively inert". It explains nothing and rules nothing out.

Mugg's replacement is a soundboard. One system, not two, with many settings that move on their own — knobs that slide, switches that flip. Speed is one setting. Effort is another. Nothing forces them to move together, so fast-and-careful thinking needs no second mind to explain it.

Then the book turns. Its second half is about belief: how beliefs form, what the implicit bias results really show, whether believing is something we choose. The bet is that tying a theory of belief to a picture of the machine makes that theory testable too — indirectly, because the machine can be tested.

Here the skeptic lands a real punch, and it is the reviewer's. If the shrunken two-system view predicts nothing that evidence can check, then no experiment can touch it. Not even Mugg's. The fight would have to be about something else: what makes two processes count as two different kinds at all. No lab settles that.

And the retreat may simply be good science. A theory that drops claims once they are disproved is behaving well. The reviewer reaches for Lakatos's name for a programme that survives by predicting less and less. Then comes the hedge: it is fair to worry the two-system view is decaying that way. It is not proven that it is.

The second punch is quieter. Mugg admits some of the belief theories he attacks could be restated in soundboard terms. If the soundboard fits all of them, then proving one of them right proves nothing about the soundboard.

The review does not dismiss the book. Plenty of theories of belief still lean on the old, disproved version of the two-system story, and showing that is worth doing. But the book promises a sustained case against two systems and an argument from evidence for one. What it delivers, the review says, is a book about belief — which is exactly what the title said it would be.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: The bold two-system story said fast, automatic and gut-level travel together. Researchers found thinking that is fast but careful, and slow but gut-level, and the packs came apart.
What survives is thinner: one kind of thinking uses working memory, the other does not. Easier to hold, and much harder to test.
The soundboard swaps two boxes for one system of knobs and switches that move on their own. But a frame that fits every theory of belief cannot be proved right by any one of them.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Two pictures of the mind that predict the same results can still be at war. That is the moment the fight has quietly stopped being about evidence.

recall.q: The two-system view survived by shrinking its claim. Why does the reviewer say that also puts it beyond the reach of Mugg's argument?
recall.a: The surviving version rests on one property and predicts almost nothing, so no experiment can disprove it — and Mugg's case is built from evidence. What is left is a question about when two processes count as two different kinds, and no result can settle that.

cards.title: Mass shootings and suicides peak in the same weeks
cards.body: Across nearly eight years of United States data, mass shootings and deaths by suicide rose and fell together across the calendar — both highest in mid-summer, both lowest in mid-winter, with the two peaks landing about ten days apart. It is one study, and it measured only timing. Its authors are firm that it does not show one kind of violence causes the other.
cards.evidence: single study · 3,305 mass shootings, 360,827 suicide deaths · US records 2014–2021 · timing only, no cause tested

sections.text:
Count the mass shootings in an American January and you get about four. Count them in a July and you get about thirty-one. The gap repeats year after year — and it has a twin: deaths by suicide climb and fall across the calendar on almost the same schedule.

That much is solid. Two researchers, Mark É. Czeisler and Charles A. Czeisler, took nearly eight years of United States data — January 2014 to October 2021 — and looked only at the shape of the year. Mass shooting here means an incident where four or more people, not counting the shooter, were shot, whether they died or lived.

Both curves peak in mid-summer and bottom out in mid-winter. The models put the suicide peak near June 23 and the mass-shooting peak near July 3, ten days apart. June, July and August run high for both; December, January and February run low for both.

The two summers are not the same size. Suicide deaths rise about 12 percent from the winter low, roughly 3,439 a month to 3,845. Mass shootings rise about 613 percent, from about 4.4 a month to 31.3 — but a percentage swells when the starting number is tiny, and this is a small count multiplying, not thousands of extra events.

What nobody knows is why. This is a single study, and it was not built to find a cause. It can show that two things move together across the year; it cannot show that one moves the other. Czeisler says so directly: the finding does not demonstrate that suicides cause mass shootings, or the reverse.

The idea it feeds is older and still argued. Some mass-shooting researchers, reading case files, have proposed that many attacks are final acts — homicidal and suicidal at once. Two facts sit near that claim.

Depression is worst in the dark winter months, yet suicide deaths peak in summer; a 2019 study of psychiatric patients found the most lethal attempts peaking in summer while milder attempts and general depression did not. And most mass shooters are adult men, the group with the highest suicide rate.

Matching seasons fit the final-act idea. They do not test it. Summer heat, the social demands of summer, and seasonal shifts in irritability or impulsiveness are candidates too, and one study of timing cannot separate them.

The clean test would be the Southern Hemisphere, where summer falls in December and January. If the rhythm flipped with the seasons there, the seasonal explanation would gain real weight. Czeisler notes why that test cannot be run: mass shootings are rare enough outside the United States that there is nothing to compare.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text:
Mass shooting counts came from the Gun Violence Archive, an independent database built from police, government and media reports. Suicide deaths came from CDC mortality records. In total, 3,305 mass shootings and 360,827 deaths by suicide.

The researchers made every month the same length before comparing them, then used models to strip out the long-term rise in these events, leaving only the within-year rhythm. That is the whole method: one study, one country, one stretch of years, and no attempt at cause.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
There is no official national count of mass shootings in the United States, so the totals depend on an independent database and on where the definition is drawn. Move that line and the numbers move with it. The 2021 suicide figures were provisional — still being counted — and may be an undercount.

The pattern held steadily from 2014 through 2019. Then 2020 behaved oddly: the mass-shooting summer spike grew sharper while the suicide summer peak shrank, which the authors put down to the disruption of the early pandemic. A single study that finds a shape has not yet found a reason.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Knowing when is not knowing why. It is still enough to be ready in May.

recall.q: The two curves peak about ten days apart, every year. Why does that still not show that one kind of violence drives the other?
recall.a: Because the study measured only timing. Moving together across the calendar is consistent with shared triggers — the final-act idea, summer heat, the social demands of summer, seasonal shifts in impulsiveness — but a single study of when things happen cannot separate those, and its authors say it does not test the mechanism.

cards.title: Is 'representation' a thing in the head, or a way to talk?
cards.body: A state in a toad's brain fires just before its tongue shoots out. Ask what that state means and you get two good answers — a moving worm-shaped object, or food — and a philosopher argues no physical fact can pick between them. If she is right, the representations that cognitive science is built on are a useful way of talking, not furniture inside the head.

sections.text:
Drag a small dark blob sideways past a toad. The tongue shoots out. It does not matter whether the blob is food — experiments show a toad will gobble up anything moving and worm-shaped, nutritious or not.

Just before the tongue goes, a state fires in the toad's optic tectum, a visual part of its brain. Call it V. What does V stand for — and is standing-for a real thing that happens inside a skull, or only something we say about it?

Position A is the Representational Theory of Mind, and it means this literally. Every belief, every concept, every perception contains a mental representation: an inner item that is about something outside it. They come in many shapes — sentence-like, picture-like, maps, simulations, the place cells that track where an animal is.

This is not offered as a handy description. The mind really is stocked with such items, and the processes cognitive science studies really do run on them. Most defenders want one thing more: to explain "X represents Y" in purely physical terms, borrowing no words about meaning or purpose. Nobody has finished that job, though many think it is slowly coming together.

Position B is Frances Egan's: the job cannot be finished, because content is never forced by the facts. Take V. Karen Neander argues it represents a moving worm-shaped object rather than a nutrient, and her reason is strong — movement and worm-shape are what trigger the tongue, while being nutritious does no causal work at all. It merely tags along.

But a biologist asking how the toad survives in its patch of the world has an equally strong reason to say V represents food. No physical fact separates the two readings. What separates them is what you are trying to explain.

So Egan splits science in two. There is the theory proper: a mechanism takes in visual information about a distant object and puts out a tongue. Then there is the gloss scientists lay on top — naming one state a representation, saying it stands for the worm. The gloss is not idle: it tracks the real causal story and makes it usable, since the neuron-by-neuron version would be impossibly complex.

But it is a way of talking, and more than one gloss fits. Beliefs get the same treatment — states with the right causal roles, mapped onto sentences; near-beliefs rather than beliefs.

The crux is narrow. No new toad experiment settles it. What would settle it is a single physical fact that picks worm-shaped object over food and rules the other out, without leaning on what the scientist happens to want explained. Egan says no such fact exists.

Her reviewer, Christopher Hill, calls the book "a font of fresh ideas", says he learned a great deal from it, and is not persuaded. Egan's argument assumes there is only one representing relation, so the two answers must compete. Drop that assumption and allow two — one for causal machinery, one for ecological significance, each explainable in physical terms.

Then both answers are true at once, and picking one is just a scientist choosing which true thing to say. Scientists do that every day without deflating their theories. Hill's second worry cuts deeper: Egan treats mental content as suspect, then helps herself to sentences with full-blown meaning to build her mapping. If a sentence can have truth conditions, why not a thought?

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: The representational theory is meant literally: beliefs, concepts and perceptions contain inner items that are about the world, and cognitive science runs its explanations over those items.
Egan's wedge is the toad. One brain state reads as 'moving worm-shaped object' to someone explaining the mechanism, and as 'food' to someone explaining survival. The physics does not choose.
Her repair: separate the theory proper, which is the physical mechanism, from the gloss that calls a state a representation. The gloss earns its keep by being usable, not by being literally true.
Hill's reply: allow two representing relations instead of one, causal and ecological, and both readings of the toad become true together — explained in physical terms, with nothing deflated.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The argument was never about what the toad's brain says. It is about whether anything in a brain says anything at all.

recall.q: Neander and an ecologist read the same toad brain state two different ways. Why does Egan treat that as a problem for the whole representation project?
recall.a: Because the choice between 'moving worm-shaped object' and 'food' is settled by what the scientist wants to explain, not by any physical fact. If content gets picked for practical reasons, it was never explained in purely physical terms — and that was the project's promise.

cards.title: The part of maths that proofs leave out
cards.body: A machine writes a correct proof of a hard unsolved problem. The problem is closed, and nobody understands it any better. Grant Sanderson says mathematicians have always done a second kind of work — showing why an idea had to be that idea — and that the field has never given it real credit. He wants that work to have a name, and a status.

sections.text:
Someone new to computers prints out the first ten thousand prime numbers. The list is correct. It is also useless to them. Bill Thurston used that small story to make a point about his own field: what people want from mathematics is almost never a pile of answers.

The common belief runs the other way. Mathematics is proofs. A mathematician's job is to prove what nobody has proved yet. The lectures, the textbooks, the talk at the blackboard — pleasant extras around the real work. And the belief makes sense: a proof either exists or it does not, so progress can be counted. Nothing else in the field is that clean.

It is still wrong about what mathematicians do, and machines that write proofs have made the mistake easy to see. In April this year Liam Price sent in a solution to Erdős Problem 1196, a problem specialists called both important and hard to crack. It came out of his back-and-forth with GPT-5.4 Pro. A proof now existed. Human understanding had barely moved.

Two mathematicians, Nat Sothanaphan and Jared Lichtman, worked out what the machine had done and rewrote it so people could read it. In May, eight authors published a paper opening up the idea underneath — and that idea cleared up not just that problem but a cluster around it, including a cleaner proof of the Erdős Primitive Set Conjecture. Ticking off one more problem was never the value. We understand primitive sets better now than we did at the start of 2026.

Sanderson has a name for that second kind of work: a motivated explanation. He does not mean making maths simple for the public. He means any work whose main aim is to answer one question — "how would you think of that?" — even when the material is so hard that only experts can follow it.

The trick is to flip the order. In a proof, the definitions come first: you put a new object on the table, then study what it does. In a motivated explanation they sit in the middle — the new object comes in only after the problem it solves has been laid out. A proof needs every line to be correct. An explanation is often better when it starts with an idea that is not quite right, lets it break, then repairs it, because that is where ideas come from.

None of this is new. Thurston spent years on work he himself filed as earning no credit: a book written to a high standard of communication, teaching, a research institute, a short film. Timothy Gowers gave about half his working time for five years to editing the Princeton Companion to Mathematics. He says plainly that he would probably not have been offered the job without his Fields Medal.

That is why the proof-only story keeps winning. Credit follows what can be checked. So the celebrated record fills with proofs, so outsiders decide that proofs are the field — and permission to do the other work arrives, if it arrives at all, after the medal. Sanderson's fix is to give explanation the standing of a problem: something you can pose, work on, and solve. Right now, every proof a machine writes is born as an unsolved explanation problem.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The case for leaving things alone is strong. Two mathematicians can check a proof line by line and agree. An explanation cannot be checked that way, and Sanderson admits it: no software will ever verify an explanation the way it verifies a proof. Hang hiring and tenure on a judgement that soft, one commenter warns, and those calls turn subjective and political. A harder objection: if machines can write proofs, why would they not write the textbooks too? Sanderson's answer is that the soft measure is the price of taking the human side of the field seriously — and that asking whether an idea is motivated is not so far from asking whether a step follows.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A field rarely gets to decide out loud what counts as real work. Mathematics is deciding now — which makes this the most interesting moment in a lifetime to walk into it.

recall.q: A machine-assisted proof of Erdős Problem 1196 already existed. Why did the work that came after it matter more?
recall.a: The proof closed the question without teaching anyone anything. The work after it pulled out the idea underneath and showed that idea cleared up a whole cluster of nearby problems, including a cleaner proof of the Primitive Set Conjecture. That is Sanderson's point: a proof ticks the box, an explanation is what moves understanding.
